newsitem.title: UK: Britain's election -- facts and figures.
newsitem.headline: Britain's election -- facts and figures.

text.p: Facts and figures about Britain's May 1 election:

Prime Minister John Major's centre-right Conservative Party will be seeking an unprecedented fifth consecutive term, but is lagging more than 20 points behind the main opposition Labour Party in public opinion polls.
Labour has moved away from its socialist roots towards the centre of British politics under the leadership of Tony Blair.
The Conservatives have been in power since May 4, 1979. The last election took place on April 9, 1992.
Eligible to vote are 43.98 million out of 58 million inhabitants. The voting age is 18. Voting is not compulsory. In 1992, 77.8 percent of the electorate of 43.2 million voted.
Governments have a five-year term.
Number of seats in the House of Commons after election, 659. Seats needed for an overall majority, 330.

Parliamentary boundaries were redrawn in mid-1995 to allow for population redistribution. Eight new constituencies were formed. Only 194 constituences have unchanged boundaries. Constituencies have average of 69,000 electors.
Standings in the outgoing (651-seat) parliament.
The Conservatives had 321 seats and the combined opposition 324
Conservatives 321
Labour 272
Liberal Democrats 26
Plaid Cymru (Welsh Nationalist) 4
Ulster Unionists 9
Scottish National Party 4
United Kingdom Unionist 1
Referendum Party 1
Social and Democratic Labour Party 4
Democratic Unionist Party 3
Vacant seats 2
Speaker and three deputies 4
Total 651

Voting system. The candidate who gets most votes in each single-seat constituency wins. This first-past-the-post system favours big parties. The Liberal Democrats say reforms to introduce proportional representation are their price for joining any coalition following election.
More than 3,000 people have already put their names forward as candidates, more than in 1992 which was then a record. By the time nominations close there may be up to 5,000 candidates.

Voting at 47,000 polling stations ends at 2100 GMT on Thursday. The result may be known by 0330 GMT on Friday, when around 450 declarations will have been made, if one party has a large majority. If one party has a small majority, the result is expected around 0600. Northern Ireland's constituencies will not declare results until Friday morning.
To win outright Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing compared with the 1992 election, according to calculations by voting experts Colin Rallings and Michael Thrasher of the University of Plymouth.

Major took over as leader of the Conservative Party, and prime minister, when Margaret Thatcher stepped down in November 1990. Blair was voted in as Labour leader in July 1994 after the death of John Smith.
If no party wins outright, Queen Elizabeth as head of state would probably ask the leader of the one with most seats to try to govern.
Recent election results:
1992 - Conservatives 336 (41.9 pct of vote), Labour 271 (34.4 pct), Liberal Democrat 20, others 24. Majority 21. Turnout 77.7 percent
1987 - Conservatives 375 (42.3 pct), Labour 229 (30.8 pct), Liberal/Social Democrat Alliance 22, others 23. Majority 101. Turnout 75.3 percent. (Conservative speaker not included)
1983 - Conservatives 397 (42.4 percent), Labour 209 (27.6 percent), Social Democrat Party/Liberal alliance 23, others 21. Majority 144 (largest Conservative majority since 1935). Turnout 72.7 percent
1979 - Conservatives 339 (43.9 percent), Labour 269 (36.9 percent), Liberal 11, others 16. Majority 43. Turnout 76.0 percent
1974 (October) - Conservative 277 (35.8 percent), Labour 319 (39.2 percent), Liberal 13, others 26. Labour majority of three. Turnout 72.8 percent.
